title: SQL vs NoSQL
subtitle: Not a war — a set of tradeoffs, and what each one gave up
objectives: Say what NoSQL actually means and debunk the speed and schemaless myths
Match the four NoSQL families to the data shapes and access patterns they serve
Explain the deepest difference: model the data vs model the queries
Choose honestly — starting from access patterns and guarantees, not from fashion

exercises.prompt: What does 'NoSQL' actually mean?
choices: Databases with no query language at all
'Not only SQL' — an umbrella for non-relational databases that made different tradeoffs
Databases that are always faster than SQL ones
Databases that have no schema
exercises.why: NoSQL isn't an anti-SQL movement. It's a loose family of stores that gave up parts of the relational model to get something else — usually easier horizontal scaling or a more natural data shape.
exercises.goDeeper: The name is genuinely terrible and has fuelled a decade of confused arguments. Plenty of 'NoSQL' databases have rich query languages, and some now literally speak SQL. The useful question is never 'SQL or NoSQL' — it's 'what did this database give up, and what did it buy with it?'

exercises.prompt: Is NoSQL inherently faster than a relational database?
choices: Yes — it's newer and better engineered
No — it's faster at certain access patterns because it does less: no joins, no cross-node transactions, fewer guarantees
No — it's actually always slower
They're identical in performance
exercises.why: Speed here isn't magic, it's subtraction. A key-value store is blisteringly fast at 'give me the value at this key' precisely because that's all it promises to do.
exercises.goDeeper: Generalize this instinct: whenever one system is dramatically faster than another at a similar task, ask what it stopped promising. Performance almost always comes from removing a guarantee, not from writing better code. That question will serve you for your whole career.

exercises.prompt: A document database is often called 'schemaless.' So where did the schema go?
choices: There genuinely isn't one — the data has no shape
Into your application code — every reader must now handle every historical shape of the data
Into the operating system
It's generated automatically at runtime
exercises.why: Your data always has a shape. 'Schemaless' only means the database stopped enforcing it — so the enforcement moved into your code, where it's optional and easy to forget.
exercises.goDeeper: The real terms are schema-on-write (SQL: the database rejects malformed data at insert) versus schema-on-read (accept anything; readers cope). Schema-on-read feels liberating in month one and painful in year three, when one collection holds five generations of shape and every reader needs branches for all of them.

exercises.prompt: SQL enforces the shape of data when you ______; many NoSQL stores leave it to be interpreted when you read.
choices: write
delete
connect
backup
exercises.why: Schema-on-write catches bad data at the door, before it's stored. Schema-on-read lets it in and makes every future reader deal with it.

exercises.prompt: Which of these are TRUE of relational databases? Select all.
choices: They enforce structure and relationships for you
They're built around joining normalized tables
They cannot handle large scale under any circumstances
They give strong transactional guarantees
exercises.why: Structure, joins, and strong transactions are real. 'Can't handle scale' is the myth — a single well-tuned Postgres routinely serves workloads far beyond what most companies ever reach.
exercises.goDeeper: This myth has cost the industry enormous pain. Teams adopt a distributed NoSQL store at 5,000 users to prepare for a scale they never hit, and pay the cost of losing joins and transactions every single day in between.

exercises.prompt: So what's the genuinely useful question when picking a database?
choices: Is it SQL or NoSQL?
What will I ask of this data, what must never be wrong, and what does this database give up?
Which one is newest?
Which one does my favourite company use?
exercises.why: Access patterns and required guarantees decide the answer. The SQL/NoSQL label is a category, not a decision.
exercises.goDeeper: Notice that this question doesn't mention a single product name. If you can't answer it, no amount of benchmarking will save you — you'll just pick fast software that's wrong for your problem.

exercises.prompt: Match each NoSQL family to the shape it's built for.

pairs.right: Get/put a value by one key
Huge tables, queried by partition key

exercises.why: 'NoSQL' isn't one thing — it's four very different answers to four very different problems. Lumping them together is most of why the debate is so muddled.
exercises.goDeeper: These families have less in common with each other than any of them has with Postgres. A graph database and a key-value store are about as similar as a spreadsheet and a hammer — they only share a name because of a marketing accident.

exercises.prompt: You need to store user sessions: looked up only by session id, never queried any other way. Which shape fits?
choices: Key-value
Graph
Wide-column
Relational with 6 tables
exercises.why: One access pattern, one key. A key-value store does exactly this and nothing else — which is why it's so fast at it.
exercises.goDeeper: Don't buy a relational engine to do a hashmap's job. This is the cleanest, least controversial NoSQL win there is: when your access pattern really is 'get the thing at this key,' everything else is overhead.

exercises.prompt: Sessions are read millions of times a second by one key, and can be rebuilt if lost. Add the right store, keeping Postgres as the source of truth.
exercises.why: Sessions are a single-key, rebuildable, extremely hot access pattern — exactly a key-value store's job. Postgres keeps the durable truth; Redis absorbs the volume.
exercises.goDeeper: Notice you didn't choose SQL OR NoSQL — you used both, each for what it's good at. That's polyglot persistence, and it's what most real systems actually look like. The question was never either/or.

exercises.prompt: You're storing a product catalog where every type has wildly different attributes — a book has an author, a shirt has a size, a laptop has RAM. Which fits most naturally?
choices: Key-value
Document
Graph
One relational table with 200 mostly-null columns
exercises.why: Documents are self-contained and can legitimately differ in shape from each other, which is exactly what a heterogeneous catalog is.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the strongest honest case for document stores: varied, self-contained entities you fetch whole. But be clear-eyed about the cost you just accepted — nothing now guarantees that shirts have sizes. That check moved into your code, forever.

exercises.prompt: You need 'friends of friends who like X, within 3 hops.' In SQL that's a self-join per hop. What's built for this?
choices: Key-value
Document
Graph
Wide-column
exercises.why: Graph databases store relationships as first-class citizens, so traversals don't explode into ever-deeper joins as you add hops.
exercises.goDeeper: The tell for a graph problem: your queries are about the CONNECTIONS, not the entities. If you find yourself joining a table to itself repeatedly and adding a level each time the product team asks for one more hop, you may have a graph problem wearing a relational costume.

exercises.prompt: Cassandra can absorb enormous write volume across many nodes. What's the catch?
choices: There isn't one — it's strictly better
You must know your query patterns up front: tables are designed around the partition key, and ad-hoc queries are painful or impossible
It can't actually write quickly
It only works on one machine
exercises.why: Wide-column stores buy their scale by making you commit to your access patterns in advance. The table is shaped around the query, so a new question can mean a new table.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the trade in its purest form. Cassandra will happily take a million writes a second across a hundred nodes — but the day a product manager asks a question you didn't design for, the answer may genuinely be 'we'd have to rewrite how the data is stored.'

lessons.title: Model the data vs model the queries

exercises.prompt: What's the deepest difference between relational and most NoSQL modeling?
choices: The syntax you type
SQL: model the data correctly, then query it however you like later. NoSQL: model your queries first, then shape the storage to serve them
How fast they read from disk
One uses JSON and one doesn't
exercises.why: This is the actual mental shift, and it's the thing people get wrong. Relational lets you decide the questions later; most NoSQL requires you to decide them first.
exercises.goDeeper: In relational, normalize now and you can still answer questions you haven't thought of yet — the join is your escape hatch. In NoSQL you often can't join, so you must know the questions in advance and physically store the answers in the shape you'll read them.

exercises.prompt: In DynamoDB you can't join. To show an order together with its customer's name, what do you typically do?
choices: Run two queries and join in your app
Duplicate the customer's name into the order record itself
Give up and use SQL
Store a pointer and follow it
exercises.why: You store the answer, not the ingredients. The order record carries the customer name so one read returns everything the screen needs.
exercises.goDeeper: That's denormalization. It makes reads a single fast lookup — but the name now lives in two places, which is exactly unit 5's copies problem. You've traded a consistency guarantee for read speed, on purpose.

exercises.prompt: You denormalized a user's display name into all 10,000 of their posts. They change their name. What now?
choices: One update — the database handles the rest
You must update 10,000 records, and until you finish, the system displays two different names
Nothing — old posts keep the old name and that's correct
The database refuses the change
exercises.why: You moved the work from read-time to write-time. Reads became one fast lookup; that single rename became an enormous, slow, partially-visible operation.
exercises.goDeeper: Here's the fundamental exchange rate of data modeling: normalized = cheap writes, expensive reads (you join). Denormalized = cheap reads, expensive writes plus a consistency risk. Neither side is free. You are only ever choosing which side pays.

exercises.prompt: A social feed: 99% reads, 1% writes. Slide toward your modeling choice.
exercises.rightLabel: Denormalize (store the answer, pay at write time)
exercises.why: With a 99:1 read-to-write ratio, paying at write time is obviously right: do the work once when someone posts, so that millions of reads are single cheap lookups.
exercises.goDeeper: The rule to carry: put the work where the traffic isn't. Read-heavy → precompute and denormalize. Write-heavy → normalize and compute at read time. You'll meet this exact reasoning again, by a different name, in the news feed capstone: fan-out on write vs fan-out on read.

exercises.prompt: What are the real costs of denormalizing? Select all.
choices: Copies can disagree with each other
Writes get more expensive
Reads get slower
You must know your access patterns in advance
exercises.why: Reads get FASTER — that's the entire point of doing it. The costs are drifting copies, heavier writes, and committing to your query patterns early.
exercises.goDeeper: Notice that two of those three costs are the same cost wearing different hats: once data lives in many places, both writing it and trusting it get harder. Duplication is never just a storage decision.

exercises.prompt: Your NoSQL data model can answer every question your product asks today. What's the risk?
choices: There's no risk — it works
Tomorrow's question may not fit the shape you committed to, and reshaping stored data is far harder than writing a new query
It will run out of disk
It can't be backed up
exercises.why: Modeling for your queries means your storage encodes today's questions. A new question can require reshaping the data itself — not just writing new SQL.
exercises.goDeeper: This is the asymmetry that decides most real arguments: in relational, a new question costs you a query. In query-modeled NoSQL, a new question can cost you a migration. Early products change their questions constantly — which is a strong hint about what to default to.

exercises.prompt: Why is a relational database genuinely hard to scale across many machines?
choices: The software is old and poorly written
Joins and ACID transactions across machines require network coordination — which is slow and complex. Many NoSQL stores scale easily precisely because they dropped those
Because it writes to disk
Licensing restrictions
exercises.why: This is the honest technical reason, not marketing. A join is cheap when both tables sit on one machine and brutal when the rows live on different servers across a network.
exercises.goDeeper: So 'NoSQL scales better' really means: 'we removed the features that are hard to distribute.' That's a genuine engineering achievement AND a genuine loss. Just be certain you know which half you're buying — people usually notice the achievement and discover the loss later.

exercises.prompt: Which are legitimate reasons to reach for NoSQL? Select all.
choices: One well-known access pattern at massive scale
Data that's naturally self-contained documents
Relational feels old-fashioned
You need writes distributed across many nodes and don't need cross-node transactions
exercises.why: Known access patterns at scale, document-shaped data, and distributed writes without cross-node transactions are all real reasons. Fashion is not a reason.
exercises.goDeeper: Note what all three real reasons have in common: they're statements about your workload, not about the technology. Every good database decision is really a description of your problem.

exercises.prompt: New product. You don't yet know what queries you'll need, and you have 1,000 users. Sane default?
choices: Cassandra, to be ready for scale later
A relational database — flexible about questions you haven't thought of, constraints for free, and far more headroom than you need
MongoDB, because JSON is convenient
A graph database, since everything is connected
exercises.why: At 1,000 users your bottleneck isn't the database — it's not yet knowing what you're building. Relational lets you change your questions cheaply, which is precisely what early products do constantly.
exercises.goDeeper: 'You're not Google' isn't an insult, it's an engineering fact. A single well-tuned Postgres routinely handles tens of thousands of transactions per second and terabytes of data. Most teams who chose NoSQL 'for scale' hit the pain of losing joins years before they'd have hit Postgres's ceiling.

exercises.prompt: Which statement is TRUE about the SQL/NoSQL landscape today?
choices: NoSQL databases never support transactions
The lines have blurred: Postgres stores and indexes JSON, MongoDB added transactions, and NewSQL systems aim for relational semantics with horizontal scale
SQL databases cannot store JSON
The two worlds remain completely separate
exercises.why: The clean 2010s dichotomy has largely dissolved. Both sides absorbed the other's best ideas, and NewSQL (Spanner, CockroachDB) explicitly chases both at once.
exercises.goDeeper: Which is why the honest modern answer is rarely 'SQL or NoSQL.' It's: what access patterns, what guarantees, what scale — and can my boring default already handle it? Most real systems end up polyglot anyway: Postgres for truth, Redis for hot reads, S3 for blobs. It's a toolbox, not a religion.

exercises.prompt: A team picked NoSQL 'for scale.' A year later they need a report that requires joining across two collections. What happens?
choices: It's trivial — they just write the query
They must denormalize (taking on the update burden), join in application code (slow, N+1), or migrate — the flexibility they gave up is exactly what they now need
The database adds joins automatically
Nothing changes
exercises.why: This is the most common real-world regret in database choice. They optimized for a scale problem they might have, and gave up flexibility for a problem they definitely had.
exercises.goDeeper: Joining in application code is the worst of all worlds: you get unit 3's N+1 problem, over a network, with no query optimizer helping you — and you rebuild, badly, the exact feature you chose to give up.

exercises.prompt: You're storing financial transactions for a bank. Slide toward your choice.
exercises.why: Money needs invariants the database itself enforces and multi-row transactions that genuinely hold. Here correctness dwarfs scale — and being wrong isn't a bug, it's a regulator.
exercises.goDeeper: Contrast with the social feed slider two lessons ago, which went the opposite way. Same question, opposite answers — because the cost of being wrong is completely different. That cost, not the technology, is what's actually choosing.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest way to choose a database?
choices: Pick whatever's trending this year
Start from access patterns and required guarantees; default to relational unless a specific need pushes you off it — and know exactly what you're giving up
Always NoSQL — it's the future
Always SQL — NoSQL is a fad
exercises.why: Start from the problem: what will you ask, and what must never be wrong. Then pick the boring default unless something concrete — scale profile, data shape, write distribution — forces you off it, consciously.
exercises.goDeeper: Look back at this whole unit: every answer reduced to the same two questions — what will you ask of the data, and what must never be wrong? Technology names came last, every single time. That ordering is the actual skill; everything else is trivia.
